Although Apple has long championed privacy as a selling point of its hardware and services, I can't help but wonder whether Apple now regrets introducing a privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

For a measure with a relatively limited scope of impact, it sometimes feels as though almost every month brings a new antitrust lawsuit or regulatory challenge against it. A third lawsuit targeting ATT is being filed in the UK — and this time, there's a new twist.

This article has been updated to include Apple's response at the end…

The personalised advertising controversy

Personalised advertising has been a hot topic in the tech world for years. The ads we see are no longer random products that may or may not interest us, but rather are displayed based on our interests — gathered through the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win-win situation for everyone. Consumers see ads they may actually be interested in; advertisers get better returns on their ad spending through precise targeting; and free apps and websites funded by advertising also earn more for the same reason.

Although the data used to deliver personalised ads is collected anonymously, the practice has led to widespread public perception that it is an invasion of privacy. Even though Apple developed a specific technology to ensure data anonymity, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency aims to address this issue by letting consumers choose whether their data can be used to deliver personalised ads. Developers who wish to collect such data must obtain consumer consent.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, this has triggered a series of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, mainly centring on one fact: Apple's own apps do not need to seek this consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules are actually consistent: Apple's own apps do not display the ATT prompt because they do not collect the data covered by ATT. Third-party apps that do not collect such data are likewise exempt and do not need to display the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints brought before the UK's relevant antitrust regulator — the Competition Appeal Tribunal. Apple lost the first lawsuit (currently under appeal), and the second is still ongoing.

Reuters reported on the latest lawsuit filed today.

A new twist

This latest lawsuit has an interesting twist: the plaintiff is Ann Pope, who was previously a senior official at the regulator behind this case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, is leading the lawsuit. She said Apple's policies "have caused very significant harm to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." Pope said in a statement: "This action is vital to protecting the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, ensuring the rules Apple implements are fair, and compensating UK companies for the losses they have suffered."

Following a recent investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator, Apple agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU. Regarding the lawsuit, Apple responded to us as follows:

Over the years, many privacy advocates have publicly voiced their support for ATT.
